answer:
Evidence from multiple sources supports the claim that scanned PDFs can weaken citation quality:

- Scanned, image-only PDFs without an embedded text layer cause TutorChat to either return answers with no source citations or point citations to page 1 of a large document rather than a specific section [NL-021#NL-021-S02].
- A customer reported that 60% of clinical documentation is scanned PDFs, and for those files citation mapping still fails, citing page one of a 150-page document instead of the actual checklist page [NL-018#NL-018-S04].
- Remaining citation tickets in May and June are almost entirely linked to scanned, image-only PDFs, where TutorChat struggles to establish citation anchors and often links to the start of the file rather than the specific page [NL-011#NL-011-S05].
- Scanned PDFs require OCR; without OCR, no text is extracted and citations cannot be generated, while blurry or low-resolution scans can cause broken citations that fail to link to the exact paragraph [NL-006#NL-006-S03].
- A common cause of "No citation available" or broken links is that the answer came from a low-resolution scanned PDF and the layout parser could not determine the exact page or section ID [NL-006#NL-006-S04].
- Scanned PDFs are flagged with low citation confidence (e.g., 45%) compared to natively digital files (100%), with a recommendation to re-upload with high-resolution OCR; the UI warning states that ingesting scanned or image-only files without OCR may result in poor citation quality [NL-021#NL-021-S05].
- Low-quality scanned PDFs can cause the system to struggle to generate page-specific citations due to OCR limitations [NL-028#NL-028-S03].
